title: Lap 3 — Dynatrace Assist & AI
description: Learn how to use natural language with Dynatrace — Playground, Copilot, and Local MCP.
imagine: Your team wants to start writing DQL and querying Dynatrace using natural language. You need to know which approach fits which situation — and which one is right for you today.
yourGoal: Answer 5 questions about the three ways ANZ can use Dynatrace Assist and AI — understanding the trade-offs, setup requirements, and the right tool for each use case.
tools: Dynatrace Assist · Dynatrace Playground · Microsoft Copilot · Local MCP Server
note: These questions are based on the 'Dynatrace Assist at Your Fingertips' notebook. Focus on the approach and trade-offs for each option — not the specific prompts or commands.

story.introduction: Dynatrace Assist brings natural language directly into your observability workflow. But there are three distinct ways to access it — each with different setup, capability, and trade-offs.
story.context: From zero-setup playground access through to a fully environment-aware Local MCP server connected to your live tenant, understanding the options means you can choose the right entry point for your team today — and grow from there.

questions.title: Ways to use natural language with Dynatrace
questions.content: How can ANZ team members interact with Dynatrace using natural language to write and run DQL queries?

options.text: Access Dynatrace Assist on playground.apps.dynatrace.com
options.explanation: This is one valid option, but not the only one.

options.text: Use Dynatrace AI skills within Microsoft Copilot
options.explanation: This is one valid option, but not the only one.

options.text: Connect an Local MCP client with Dynatrace AI skills in their IDE
options.explanation: This is one valid option, but not the only one.

options.text: All of the above
options.explanation: Correct. The notebook covers three complementary approaches: Playground, Self-Help Copilot (M365), and Local MCP Server. Each builds on the last in terms of setup and capability.

questions.explanation: Dynatrace Assist is accessible via three paths — Playground for zero-friction exploration, Copilot for DQL drafting, and Local MCP Server for full environment-aware access. The right choice depends on your team's setup and goals.
hints: The notebook presents multiple options — consider whether any single option alone covers all the ways described.

questions.title: Zero-setup entry point
questions.content: Which option lets you explore Dynatrace Assist immediately — with zero setup, no tenant credentials, and access to pre-loaded demo data?

options.text: Self-Help Copilot
options.explanation: Self-Help Copilot requires light setup — cloning a repository and adding it to your Copilot workspace.

options.text: Local MCP Server
options.explanation: Local MCP Server requires moderate setup including Node.js, repository cloning, and browser-based authentication.

options.text: Dynatrace Playground
options.explanation: Correct. The Playground at playground.apps.dynatrace.com requires no setup, no credentials, and is pre-loaded with realistic demo data — ready in ~2 minutes.

options.text: K8s Optimization Report
options.explanation: The K8s Optimization Report requires live telemetry from your own environment — it is the payoff, not the starting point.

questions.explanation: Playground is the fastest path to experiencing Dynatrace Assist. Because it uses shared demo data, it is not environment-aware — but that makes it ideal for learning the patterns before applying them to live data.
hints: Look at the Setup column in the comparison table — one option shows 'None'.

questions.title: Local MCP Server advantage
questions.content: What is the key advantage of the Local MCP Server approach over Playground and Self-Help Copilot?

options.text: It requires no setup and works immediately
options.explanation: Local MCP Server requires moderate setup — Node.js, a cloned repository, and browser authentication.

options.text: It generates DQL locally without any live connection
options.explanation: That describes the Self-Help Copilot approach, not Local MCP Server.

options.text: It is fully environment-aware — querying and generating against your live ANZ tenant data
options.explanation: Correct. The Local MCP Server connects your IDE directly to your Dynatrace tenant, scoped to your user permissions. It can build dashboards, run notebooks, and execute DQL against live telemetry.

options.text: It works offline without any credentials
options.explanation: Local MCP Server requires browser-based OAuth authentication to connect to your tenant.

questions.explanation: The Local MCP Server is the most powerful option because it is environment-aware. Your IDE assistant can generate and execute DQL against your actual data, create notebooks, and build dashboards — all scoped to your own user permissions.
hints: Look at the 'Environment-aware' column in the comparison table — which option shows a green tick with 'Browser auth'?

questions.title: Self-Help Copilot trade-off
questions.content: When using the Self-Help Copilot approach, what is the key trade-off to understand?

options.text: It requires admin rights to provision platform tokens
options.explanation: The Self-Help Copilot approach runs entirely local — no tokens or admin rights are needed.

options.text: It generates DQL locally but is not connected to your live environment — queries must be copied and run manually in your tenant
options.explanation: Correct. Copilot uses the Dynatrace AI skills repository as a local reference to draft DQL, but it has no live connection — you copy the generated query into your tenant to execute it.

options.text: It only works inside the Dynatrace UI
options.explanation: Self-Help Copilot runs entirely on your laptop inside Microsoft Copilot — no Dynatrace UI required.

options.text: It needs a dedicated OAuth client configured in your Dynatrace tenant
options.explanation: OAuth clients are not required for the Self-Help Copilot approach.

questions.explanation: The Self-Help Copilot is great for drafting DQL fast without any live connection — ideal when you are offline or want to prototype queries. The trade-off is that you need to copy the generated DQL into your tenant to execute it and verify the results.
hints: The notebook notes that Copilot 'runs entirely local — no tenant credentials required to draft queries'. What does that imply about execution?

questions.title: Local MCP Server authentication model
questions.content: The Local MCP Server approach connects to your Dynatrace tenant. How does it authenticate?

options.text: Via a long-lived platform token stored in a config file
options.explanation: The Local MCP Server explicitly does not require platform tokens — that is one of its advantages.

options.text: Via OAuth Authorization Code flow in your browser — no token-creation rights needed
options.explanation: Correct. The Local MCP Server uses browser-based OAuth — you sign in as yourself. The token is cached securely in the OS keychain after the first login. No admin rights or token creation are needed.

options.text: Via an API key entered manually at startup
options.explanation: API keys are not used in the Local MCP Server approach.

options.text: Via SSO configured directly in your IDE
options.explanation: Authentication flows through your browser, not through IDE-level SSO.

questions.explanation: Browser-based OAuth means you sign in as yourself — scoped to your own permissions — without needing anyone to create tokens or OAuth clients for you. The token is cached in your OS keychain after the first login.
hints: The notebook explicitly says 'you don't need permission to create platform tokens or OAuth clients'. How does it authenticate instead?

learningObjectives: Identify the three ways to use natural language with Dynatrace
Choose the right Dynatrace Assist approach based on setup constraints and use case
Understand the trade-off of the Self-Help Copilot — DQL drafting without live execution
Explain why the Local MCP Server is the most powerful option and how it authenticates
Know which option requires zero setup and why that matters for adoption
